findings.message: Each chamber's arch spans its depth, along the draft, so its thrust falls on the walls before and behind it, not on the side walls. The walls between chambers take the arches either side, which push against each other (Olsen p.94–95); the front and back walls each take one arch's thrust, 1,102 lb hot across the kiln's width. Brace them: Olsen calls bracing a chamber kiln's firebox and front chamber 'a must' (p.97). No source here sizes that bracing, so no steel frame is sized; or hold the ends with masonry (roof.buttressed).
findings.reference: Olsen, The Kiln Book, 4th ed., p.94–95 (the arches throw their thrust onto the common wall), p.97 (bracing a chamber kiln's firebox and front chamber 'is a must')

findings.message: Fireboxes are built of the kiln's own layers, the walls' round their sides and over their roofs, the floor's under them, unless the design gives one its own lining (firebox.lining, where the book builds it of other brick). Against a wall, the grate sits its step below the chamber floor, so smouldering coals fall into the front stacking (p.188), and the inlet flues are cut at the floor's level in the wall between; below the kiln's floor the firebox has walls of its own. Stoke holes are cut with their foot at the grate (p.188), and ash pits are left open at the mouth (p.188). The roofs are drawn of the walls' layers laid flat: span a flat one with an arch, bricks or kiln shelves as Olsen does (p.145), or give it a corbel roof. Firebox 1, against the front wall, drawn 14 in tall, as wide as it is, as its height isn't given, drawn with its grate level with the chamber floor, as no step is given; Firebox 2, a trough sunk in chamber 2's floor along its front, drawn 14 in tall, as wide as it is, as its height isn't given.
findings.reference: Olsen, The Kiln Book, 4th ed., p.92, p.141, p.145, p.188

findings.message: Firebox 1: 14 in above the grate and an ash pit 15 in below it (52% of its height below the grate), the grate 0 in below the chamber floor. How high to set the grate depends on the firing wanted. Olsen sets it at the vertical midpoint (Fig. 8-2, p.199–200; the Breda kiln's equal volumes above and below, p.167); for the most heat his fast-fire kilns put more than half below, for the most air under the coals (p.140, p.204); a grate set too low chokes the coals (p.199). A 9–12 in rise from the grate to the chamber floor drops smouldering coals into the front stacking (p.188), and Fig. 7-3 steps up 12–15 in (p.179). Kilns fired for ash glazing and flashing make the firebox part of the first chamber, so the ash rides up round the pots: a step of 0 in, the default. This kiln is 251 ft³; Olsen's 12–18 in below and above is for 30–100 ft³ kilns (p.199), and the shortest he gives is 12½ in with the grate at 6–7 in, on a 12–16 ft³ fast-fire kiln.
findings.reference: Olsen, The Kiln Book, 4th ed., p.199–200 and Fig. 8-2 (the grate at the vertical midpoint; 12–18 in below and above on 30–100 ft³ kilns), p.188 (a 9–12 in rise from the grate to the chamber floor), p.179 (a 12–15 in step up)

findings.message: Firebox 2: 14 in above the grate and an ash pit 15 in below it (52% of its height below the grate). How high to set the grate depends on the firing wanted. Olsen sets it at the vertical midpoint (Fig. 8-2, p.199–200; the Breda kiln's equal volumes above and below, p.167); for the most heat his fast-fire kilns put more than half below, for the most air under the coals (p.140, p.204); a grate set too low chokes the coals (p.199). A 9–12 in rise from the grate to the chamber floor drops smouldering coals into the front stacking (p.188), and Fig. 7-3 steps up 12–15 in (p.179). This kiln is 251 ft³; Olsen's 12–18 in below and above is for 30–100 ft³ kilns (p.199), and the shortest he gives is 12½ in with the grate at 6–7 in, on a 12–16 ft³ fast-fire kiln.
findings.reference: Olsen, The Kiln Book, 4th ed., p.199–200 and Fig. 8-2 (the grate at the vertical midpoint; 12–18 in below and above on 30–100 ft³ kilns), p.188 (a 9–12 in rise from the grate to the chamber floor), p.179 (a 12–15 in step up)

findings.message: The 2 chambers stand in a row, each wall between them 9 in thick, as the design gives it (lining.between). Each chamber's arch spans along the draft, over its depth, and throws its thrust onto the walls before and behind it, as in Olsen's climbing kilns (p.94–95). Where an arch meets its neighbour over the wall they share, it is cut there and counted by volume. Each wall between chambers has 4 flue holes 4½ in wide and 9 in tall at the higher chamber's floor, 9 in apart: Olsen's standard 4½ × 9 in flues for the Kyoto climbing kilns, "at 9 in" read as a 9 in separator (p.96, p.45); the book doesn't say which way the 4½ in runs, so it is taken across. They are cut from the brick count. Lay them on a header course with the header over each one laid so it can be knocked out if the flue proves too small, and size them against your firing: Olsen errs on flues too large (p.45).
findings.reference: run_parts.py; Olsen, The Kiln Book, 4th ed., p.94–95; kiln-reference.md, Tube and climbing chamber kilns, p.45, p.96

The end walls take the arches' thrust; no steel for them is sized (the frame's findings).

findings.message: Brick counts assume dry joints at the nominal 9 × 4½ × 2½ in size, a ⅛ in saw cut, and 5 % extra for breakage. Each cut piece already takes its own brick in the count. The size is sourced; the saw cut is an assumption no source gives, so adjust it to your saw. The allowance is the masonry estimators' "at least 5 percent" (BIA): set allowances.brick in the design from your own experience. The side walls run through, past the end walls and the walls between chambers, which fit between them.
findings.reference: 9 × 4½ × 2½ in straight; electric-and-thermal.md §5 [S54]; kerf assumed; brick-waste.md §1, BIA Technical Note 10 (2009), p.11 [W1]

findings.message: Fireboxes are built of the kiln's own layers, the walls' round their sides and over their roofs, the floor's under them, unless the design gives one its own lining (firebox.lining, where the book builds it of other brick). Against a wall, the grate sits its step below the chamber floor, so smouldering coals fall into the front stacking (p.188), and the inlet flues are cut at the floor's level in the wall between; below the kiln's floor the firebox has walls of its own. Stoke holes are cut with their foot at the grate (p.188), and ash pits are left open at the mouth (p.188). The roofs are drawn of the walls' layers laid flat: span a flat one with an arch, bricks or kiln shelves as Olsen does (p.145), or give it a corbel roof. Firebox 1, against the front wall, drawn 14 in tall, as wide as it is, as its height isn't given, drawn with its grate level with the chamber floor, as no step is given; Firebox 2, a trough sunk in chamber 2's floor along its front, drawn 14 in tall, as wide as it is, as its height isn't given.
findings.reference: Olsen, The Kiln Book, 4th ed., p.92, p.141, p.145, p.188

findings.message: Firebox 1: 14 in above the grate and an ash pit 15 in below it (52% of its height below the grate), the grate 0 in below the chamber floor. How high to set the grate depends on the firing wanted. Olsen sets it at the vertical midpoint (Fig. 8-2, p.199–200; the Breda kiln's equal volumes above and below, p.167); for the most heat his fast-fire kilns put more than half below, for the most air under the coals (p.140, p.204); a grate set too low chokes the coals (p.199). A 9–12 in rise from the grate to the chamber floor drops smouldering coals into the front stacking (p.188), and Fig. 7-3 steps up 12–15 in (p.179). Kilns fired for ash glazing and flashing make the firebox part of the first chamber, so the ash rides up round the pots: a step of 0 in, the default. This kiln is 251 ft³; Olsen's 12–18 in below and above is for 30–100 ft³ kilns (p.199), and the shortest he gives is 12½ in with the grate at 6–7 in, on a 12–16 ft³ fast-fire kiln.
findings.reference: Olsen, The Kiln Book, 4th ed., p.199–200 and Fig. 8-2 (the grate at the vertical midpoint; 12–18 in below and above on 30–100 ft³ kilns), p.188 (a 9–12 in rise from the grate to the chamber floor), p.179 (a 12–15 in step up)

findings.reference: Olsen, The Kiln Book, 4th ed., p.199–200 and Fig. 8-2 (the grate at the vertical midpoint; 12–18 in below and above on 30–100 ft³ kilns), p.188 (a 9–12 in rise from the grate to the chamber floor), p.179 (a 12–15 in step up)

findings.message: The 2 chambers stand in a row, each wall between them 9 in thick, as the design gives it (lining.between). Each chamber's arch spans along the draft, over its depth, and throws its thrust onto the walls before and behind it, as in Olsen's climbing kilns (p.94–95). Where an arch meets its neighbour over the wall they share, it is cut there and counted by volume. Each wall between chambers has 4 flue holes 4½ in wide and 9 in tall at the higher chamber's floor, 9 in apart: Olsen's standard 4½ × 9 in flues for the Kyoto climbing kilns, "at 9 in" read as a 9 in separator (p.96, p.45); the book doesn't say which way the 4½ in runs, so it is taken across. They are cut from the brick count. Lay them on a header course with the header over each one laid so it can be knocked out if the flue proves too small, and size them against your firing: Olsen errs on flues too large (p.45).
findings.reference: run_parts.py; Olsen, The Kiln Book, 4th ed., p.94–95; kiln-reference.md, Tube and climbing chamber kilns, p.45, p.96
